thread.title: Stocks Slump Into the Weekend as Early Optimism Fades Away

title: Stocks Slump Into the Weekend as Early Optimism Fades Away
text:
Stocks Slump Into the Weekend as Early Optimism Fades Away By Nov. 2, 2018 5:29 p.m. ET Order Reprints Illustration by Michael Haddad Text size
Slouching Toward the Weekend . Stocks ended the week on a downbeat note, hurt by Apple’s (ticker: AAPL) post-earnings slump, which overshadowed early optimism about trade and jobs. In today’s After the Bell we… …see what sank early optimism; …(spoiler alert): Apple had a lot to do with it; and …note that VeriSign (VRSN) popped to its highest level since 2000 at one point.
Losing Steam
Stocks slumped on Friday, with Apple’s pain especially weighing on tech.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 109.91 points, or 0.43%, to 25270.83 while the S & P 500 slid 17.31 points, or 0.63%, to 2723.06, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 77.06 points, or 1.04%, to 7356.99. Still, all three indexes were in the black for the week.
The jobs report was a strong one, with unemployment meeting expectations and wages getting a notable bump. That may not be great for those worrying about wages or hoping for a slowdown at the Federal Reserve. Uncertainties remain. Yet “the job market is doing remarkably well, particularly this late in the expansion,” writes Plante Moran Financial Advisor’s Jim Baird. “Little seems to stand in the way of the economy finishing 2018 out on solid footing.”
Some would argue that trade is a bigger stumbling block, but we appeared to get a little bit of bright news on that front, although hopes for an agreement at the G-20 meeting may be too optimistic. “U.S.-China tensions run deep and will require more than a cheerful phone call to resolve,” notes UBS ’s Jon Gordon. Nonetheless, while an easing of tariff tensions would be a boon to the market, he doesn’t think we necessarily need it. “A global economy growing above trend, good corporate earnings data and favorable valuations relative to bonds support our overweight positioning in global equities,” he says. “A U.S.-China trade deal would provide a further boost, but it remains outside of our base case.”
Still, investors weren’t inclined to look on the bright side Friday, as Apple slid 6.6%—its biggest one-day decline since early 2014—after it issued lackluster guidance for the important year-end quarter. Nasdaq IR Intelligence’s Massud Ghaussy warns that turbulence in tech probably won’t end quickly, given tightening monetary policy making growth stocks less attractive, potential regulation and tax head winds, and slowing economic growth. While we noted that a strong report could catapult the market higher after three days of gains, the flip side of that argument was that Apple could weigh on stocks. That was the case today as the Street fretted not only about the company, its suppliers and tech in general, but also about emerging markets and less transparency . Newsletter Sign-up
That was the last thing that investors wanted to hear, given concerns about s lowing growth in China, worries heightened by Alibaba Holding ’s (BABA) results. “It’s hardly a stretch to say that the U.S. and China have entered an economic cold war,” writes Bank of America Merrill Lynch’s Joseph Quinlan. “China, in our opinion, is not headed for recession but something perhaps worse: a prolonged and fractious period with the one country in the world that not only has the economic and military firepower to block or forestall the rise of the Middle Kingdom but also is determined, at least on the surface, to do just that.”
That’s bad news for China. But given that the nation accounted for a third of global growth in 2017, “what happens in China doesn’t stay in China,” Quinlan warns. A protracted trade war threatens economic and earnings growth for both countries and the world, something that’s “finally dawning on investors,” he says. When you put it that way, it’s not surprising that markets weren’t able to break out Friday.
Still, in a scary world, many investors may still see the U.S. as the least worrisome place to be. BNP Paribas notes that while this pullback may have further to run, we’re not falling into a bear market, and with little corporate growth in Europe and a negative economic outlook for China, “strong U.S. fundamentals point to ongoing outperformance relative to the eurozone and emerging markets.”
Let’s try to remember that next week.
The Hot Stock
Verisign (VRSN) shot to the top of the S & P 500, at one point reaching its highest level since October 2000, on news it can raise prices for .com domain names.
Verisign rose $24.22, or 17.2%, to $165.02.
As MarketWatch reports, Verisign revealed in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing that it had reached an agreement with the Commerce Department to amend “the cooperative agreement to allow Verisign the flexibility to pursue with the internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (Icann) an up to 7% increase in prices for “.com” domain names in each of the last four years of each six-year period of the registry agreement.”
Year to date, Verisign is up 44.2%.
The Biggest Loser
Fortinet (FTNT) sank to the bottom of the index following a mixed third-quarter earnings report .
Fortinet lost $11.13, or 13.3%, to $72.56.
The cybersecurity firm earned 49 cents a share on revenue of $453.9 million. Analysts were looking for earnings per share of 42 cents, and revenue of $450.84 million. For the fourth quarter, it sees EPS of 50 cents to 52 cents, on revenue of $490 million to $500 million. Consensus calls for EPS of 50 cents on revenue of $492.21 million.
KeyBanc Capital Markets’ Rob Owens reiterated a Sector Weight rating on the stock, writing that “Despite the overall strength, we note this was the first quarter in two years that revenue did not beat the high end of the guided range; as such, the overall beat was the most modest over that period.”
Year to date, Fortinet is up 66.1%.
